dossiers.is-lm.title: The IS-LM model: what the state and the central bank can do
dossiers.is-lm.hook: A crisis hits. Should the state spend more? Should the central bank cut rates? Two curves are enough to understand what happens, and why it doesn't always work.
dossiers.is-lm.tldr.0: The IS-LM model sums up the short-run economy with only two quantities: output (Y) and the interest rate (i) [1].
dossiers.is-lm.tldr.1: The IS curve shows equilibrium in the goods market, the LM curve equilibrium in the money market; the economy settles where they cross.
dossiers.is-lm.tldr.2: When the state spends more, IS shifts: output rises, but so do interest rates. When the central bank creates money, LM shifts: output rises and rates fall.
dossiers.is-lm.tldr.3: In an open economy, everything depends on the exchange rate: with fixed exchange rates, fiscal policy works; with floating rates, monetary policy does, all the more so when capital moves freely [2].
dossiers.is-lm.tldr.4: Above all, the answer depends on the school: for a Keynesian, public spending revives the economy; for a monetarist, only money matters; for a new classical economist, people anticipate and stimulus is useless [11][12]. And each school dominated in a different era.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.title: Two variables, two markets
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.paragraphs.0: The model was proposed by the British economist John Hicks in 1937 to sum up Keynes's ideas in a single diagram [1]. It is a reading of Keynes by economists trained in the neoclassical school, which is why it is often called the "synthesis" of the two traditions. Here we simplify it as much as possible and look at only two variables. ==Y==, output (which is also the income of the whole country, roughly GDP). ==i==, the interest rate, that is, the price of borrowed money.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.paragraphs.1: The IS curve (goods market). When the interest rate falls, borrowing is cheaper: firms invest, households buy a car or a home on credit. Demand rises, so output rises. The lower i is, the higher Y is: the IS curve slopes down.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.paragraphs.2: The LM curve (money market). According to Keynes, people hold money for two reasons: for their ==purchases== (the higher output and incomes, the more money they need) and to ==speculate== (when rates are low, bonds yield little and risk losing value, so people prefer to hold money). When output rises, more money is needed for purchases; if the quantity of money does not change, people sell bonds to get it, bond prices fall and the interest rate rises. The higher Y is, the higher i is: the LM curve slopes up.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.paragraphs.3: Equilibrium is the point where the two curves cross: the only pair (Y, i) at which both markets are in equilibrium at the same time. Nothing guarantees that it corresponds to full employment: that is Keynes's idea, the economy can remain for a long time in an ==equilibrium with involuntary unemployment==. The rest of the course consists of shifting a curve and watching where this point goes.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.plain.title: the model in one picture
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.plain.steps.0: Picture a scale with two pans: on one side what the country produces (Y), on the other the price of borrowed money (i).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.plain.steps.1: When money is expensive (high i), people borrow less to buy a house or a machine: output falls. That is the IS curve.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.plain.steps.2: When a lot is produced (high Y), everyone needs money to pay: money becomes more expensive. That is the LM curve.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.0.plain.steps.3: The economy settles where both hold together: the equilibrium point E.
Where IS (goods) and LM (money) cross: an output level Y and an interest rate i.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.title: Fiscal policy: the state spends more
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.paragraphs.0: The state builds roads, hires, cuts taxes: it adds demand. At the same interest rate, more is produced, so ==the IS curve shifts to the right==.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.paragraphs.1: The new equilibrium is further right (Y rises) but also higher (i rises). Why do rates rise? Because more output requires more money, and because the state borrows to finance its spending.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.paragraphs.2: These higher rates discourage part of private investment: this is the ==crowding-out effect==. The stimulus works, but less than planned: output rises by less than the extra public spending, part of it is "eaten" by the rise in rates.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.paragraphs.3: A small calculation to see the idea (imaginary figures): the state spends 10 billion more. Those who receive it spend part of it, which becomes other people's income, and so on: this is the ==multiplier==, output can rise by more than 10 billion. But if rates rise and firms invest 4 billion less, that crowding-out effect has to be subtracted.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.paragraphs.4: Crowding out is weaker when investment is not very sensitive to the interest rate (a very steep IS), and it disappears in the liquidity trap, where rates do not rise.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.paragraphs.5: ==Borrowing or taxes?== If the state finances its spending by borrowing, it issues bonds: rates rise more and crowding out is stronger. If it finances it with a tax of the same amount, the effect is still positive: this is Haavelmo's ==balanced budget theorem== (in the goods market alone, output rises by the amount of spending), with weaker crowding out. And a tax cut stimulates less than a spending increase of the same amount, because households save part of it.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.plain.title: the state spends 10 billion
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.plain.steps.0: The state pays firms to renovate schools and bridges.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.plain.steps.1: These firms hire and pay wages: the workers spend at the supermarket, at restaurants…
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.plain.steps.2: The supermarket and the restaurant sell more and hire in turn: output rises by more than the 10 billion (the multiplier).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.plain.steps.3: But the state borrowed to pay, and everyone needs more money: rates rise.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.plain.steps.4: With higher rates, a small business gives up buying a new machine: this is crowding out, which trims part of the stimulus.
The economy is at point E: low output, unemployment.
IS moves right: output rises (Y↑) but so does the interest rate (i↑). Higher rates hold back private investment: crowding out.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.example.title: Example: the 2009 American stimulus plan
dossiers.is-lm.sections.1.example.text: In the middle of the financial crisis, Barack Obama signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act on 17 February 2009 [4]. Estimated cost when it was passed: 787 billion dollars over ten years, including 501 billion in spending and 286 billion in tax cuts [3]. It is the textbook case of a fiscal stimulus: shifting IS to the right to support output.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.title: Crowding out, taken apart: income effect, then crowding out
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.paragraphs.0: A fiscal stimulus works in ==two stages==, which must be kept apart. This is where crowding out takes on its full meaning.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.paragraphs.1: ==1. The income effect (the Keynesian multiplier).== First, imagine that the interest rate does not move. The state spends: the firms that receive these orders pay wages and buy from other firms; this income is partly spent and becomes the income of other households, and so on. Output goes from Y₀ to Y₁: this is point A on the diagram, on the new IS curve but at the starting rate. The larger the share of each euro earned that households consume, the stronger this effect.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.paragraphs.2: ==2. Crowding out (through the interest rate).== But the rate does not stay put. With more output, households and firms need more money for their purchases; to get it, they sell bonds. At the same time, the state issues bonds to finance its spending. Too many bonds for sale: their price falls, so ==the interest rate rises== (i₀ → i₁). At this higher rate, some investment projects are no longer profitable: firms give them up. Output falls back from Y₁ to Y₂.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.paragraphs.3: ==The result.== Final output Y₂ is higher than at the start (the stimulus works), but lower than Y₁. ==Crowding out is this gap Y₁ − Y₂==: the part of the stimulus "eaten" by private investment that disappears because of the rise in rates.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.paragraphs.4: ==What makes it strong or weak.== It is weak if investment reacts little to the interest rate (a very steep IS), or if money demand reacts strongly to the rate (a flat LM); it disappears in the liquidity trap, or if the central bank creates money at the same time (policy mix). It is total in the monetarist view (a vertical LM): all public spending replaces private spending.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.paragraphs.5: ==Other forms of crowding out==, not to be confused: in an open economy with floating exchange rates, higher rates attract capital, the currency appreciates and it is ==exports== that are crowded out; with Barro's Ricardian equivalence, households ==save== the stimulus in anticipation of future taxes [11]; and at full employment, the state and firms compete for the same workers and the same machines ("real" crowding out).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.plain.title: with (imaginary) figures to fix ideas
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.plain.steps.0: The state launches a 10-billion-euro public works plan.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.plain.steps.1: Income effect: at an unchanged rate, the wages paid are spent, then spent again… output could rise by 15 billion (point A).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.plain.steps.2: But the state borrows these 10 billion and activity requires more money: the interest rate rises by 0.5 point.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.plain.steps.3: At this rate, firms give up 5 billion of investment (a factory, machines): this is crowding out.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.plain.steps.4: In the end, output rises by 10 billion instead of 15: the stimulus worked, but a third of its effect was crowded out.
The economy is at point E: output Y₀, rate i₀.
The state spends, IS becomes IS'. If the rate stayed at i₀, output would go up to Y₁ (point A): this is the Keynesian multiplier.
The rate rises from i₀ to i₁: part of private investment disappears, output falls back from Y₁ to Y₂ (point E'). The gap Y₁ − Y₂, in red, is the crowding-out effect.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.example.title: In history: the United States in the 1980s
dossiers.is-lm.sections.2.example.text: Under Ronald Reagan, the state cut taxes and raised military spending, while Paul Volcker's Fed tightened money: the Fed's rate stayed above 14% from February to June 1982 [17]. The dollar soared and American exports suffered: crowding out through rates and through the exchange rate (see our article on Reaganomics).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.title: Monetary policy: the central bank creates money
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.paragraphs.0: The central bank (the ECB for the euro area, the Fed in the United States) can increase the quantity of money by cutting its policy rate or by buying bonds ("open market operations"). By buying bonds, it pushes their price up, and therefore the interest rate down. At the same output, money becomes more plentiful, hence cheaper: ==the LM curve shifts to the right== (or down).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.paragraphs.1: The new point is further right (Y rises) and lower (i falls). Here there is no crowding out: lower rates encourage investment and credit, which raises output. Monetary policy is all the more effective when investment reacts strongly to the interest rate.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.paragraphs.2: It can also do the opposite to cool an overheating economy or excessive inflation: less money, LM moves left, rates rise and output slows.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.plain.title: the ECB in July 2022, step by step
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.plain.steps.0: The situation: in June 2022, prices in the euro area had risen by 8.6% in one year, a record since the euro was created; energy, made more expensive by the war in Ukraine, accounted for almost half of it (4.2 points) [18].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.plain.steps.1: The decision: on 21 July 2022, the ECB raised its three policy rates by 0.5 point, its first increase since 2011, although it had signalled 0.25 [19]. It went on until its deposit rate reached 4% in September 2023 [6].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.plain.steps.2: The channel: banks refinance at a higher cost and pass the increase on. In France, the average mortgage rate went from about 1% in 2021 to 4.20% at the end of 2023 [20][21].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.plain.steps.3: For you, concretely: for €200,000 borrowed over 25 years, the monthly payment goes from about €760 (at 1.07%) to about €1,080 (at 4.2%), and the total interest cost from €28,000 to €123,000 (Geonomix calculation, excluding insurance).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.plain.steps.4: The expected effect: fewer loans, fewer home purchases and investments, so weaker demand and prices rising more slowly. In the diagram, LM moves left: i rises, Y slows.
The economy is at point E.
LM moves right: output rises (Y↑) and the interest rate falls (i↓).
LM moves left: the interest rate rises (i↑) and output slows (Y↓). This is what the ECB did in 2022-2023 against inflation.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.example.title: Example: the ECB tightens in 2022-2023
dossiers.is-lm.sections.3.example.text: Why did the ECB act? Because its mandate is price stability (inflation close to 2%), and in June 2022 inflation reached 8.6% [18]. How? By raising its deposit rate from −0.5% in July 2022 to 4% in September 2023, in ten successive hikes [6][19]. At what price? Much more expensive loans and a housing market that seized up. What the IS-LM model does not show: the effect on inflation itself, since it assumes fixed prices; it only shows that demand and output slow down.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.title: Both together: the "policy mix"
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.paragraphs.0: The two policies can be combined. If the state spends more (IS to the right) and the central bank creates money at the same time (LM to the right), output rises a lot and rates do not need to rise: the central bank prevents crowding out.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.paragraphs.1: This is what happened during Covid: states spent massively to support firms and workers, while on 18 March 2020 the ECB launched a 750-billion-euro bond-buying programme to keep rates low [7].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.paragraphs.2: Behind the policy mix lies the ==Tinbergen rule==, named after the first Nobel laureate in economics [15]: to reach two targets (for example more output AND stable rates), you need two instruments. With public spending alone, you cannot achieve both.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.paragraphs.3: The problem: the two instruments are not in the same hands. The state decides the budget, the (independent) central bank decides on money. When they pull in opposite directions, rates soar.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.plain.title: Covid, in 2020
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.plain.steps.0: Factories and shops close: output collapses.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.plain.steps.1: States pay for short-time work schemes and lend to firms: IS moves back to the right.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.plain.steps.2: At the same time, the ECB buys debt securities massively (750 billion euros announced on 18 March 2020) to keep rates low [7]: LM also moves right.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.plain.steps.3: Since rates do not rise, public stimulus does not crowd out private investment: the two policies add up.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.example.title: Example: Reagan versus Volcker, in the 1980s
dossiers.is-lm.sections.4.example.text: In the United States, President Ronald Reagan sharply cut taxes and raised military spending (IS to the right), while Paul Volcker's Fed tightened money to break inflation (LM to the left) [13][17]. The result predicted by the diagram: very high interest rates, with the Fed's rate staying above 14% from February to June 1982 [17]. Volcker himself asked the White House to reduce the deficit [13].
The economy is at point E.
IS and LM move right together: output rises strongly (Y↑↑) and the interest rate stays roughly stable.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.5.title: It all depends on the school: Keynesians versus monetarists
dossiers.is-lm.sections.5.paragraphs.0: The same diagram does not say the same thing depending on the shape given to the curves, and that choice depends on the school of thought. That is why serious economists, using the same model, recommend opposite policies.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.5.paragraphs.1: ==The Keynesian case.== For the strictest Keynesians, investment depends mainly on business confidence, not on the interest rate: the IS curve is almost vertical. Lowering rates is then useless; the state has to spend. The same is true in the liquidity trap, where LM is flat (see below).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.5.paragraphs.2: ==The monetarist case.== For Milton Friedman (Nobel Prize 1976) and the monetarists, people hold money to buy things, not to speculate: the LM curve is almost vertical [12]. The quantity of money sets output. A fiscal stimulus then only raises rates and completely crowds out private investment; only money acts, and in the long run it only raises prices.
IS is vertical: investment does not react to the interest rate.
LM goes down, rates fall… but output does not move: monetary policy is ineffective.
IS moves right: all public spending turns into output. No crowding out.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.6.title: The monetarist and neoclassical view
dossiers.is-lm.sections.6.paragraphs.0: In the monetarist view, the diagram is reversed: fiscal policy is useless in the short run and monetary policy is what works (see the diagram).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.6.paragraphs.1: The ==new classical economists== go further. Robert Lucas (Nobel Prize 1995) puts ==rational expectations== at the centre: people use all available information and are not lastingly surprised by economic policy [16]. In 1974 Robert Barro adds ==Ricardian equivalence==: if the state borrows today, households know taxes will have to be paid tomorrow, so they save what they are given, and the stimulus falls flat [11].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.6.paragraphs.2: But these results rest on strong assumptions: households who think about their children, perfect financial markets, a perfectly predictable government policy. Studies do not come down clearly for or against [11].
LM is vertical: the quantity of money sets output.
IS moves right, but only higher rates come out of it: output does not move. Crowding out is total.
LM moves right: output rises accordingly. Only money acts (and, in the long run, on prices).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.7.title: It also depends on the moment: each school had its era
dossiers.is-lm.sections.7.paragraphs.0: ==1950s-1960s: the Keynesian golden age.== The IS-LM model guides economic policy until the end of the 1960s: when unemployment rises, the state stimulates.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.7.paragraphs.1: ==1970s: stagflation.== Unemployment AND inflation at the same time, which the Keynesian model had not foreseen. The monetarists win the battle of ideas: Friedman receives the Nobel in 1976 [12], and in the early 1980s Paul Volcker's Fed tightens money to break inflation [13].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.7.paragraphs.2: ==1980s-1990s: the new classicals.== Rational expectations, distrust of stimulus, independent central banks that target price stability first [16].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.7.paragraphs.3: ==Since 2008: the return of Keynes.== With rates at zero, the liquidity trap is back: states stimulate through spending, and central banks invent new tools [5][7]. Remember: a model is a pair of glasses; you change glasses when the world changes.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.title: In an open economy: the exchange rate changes everything
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.0: In reality, a country trades with others and money flows from one country to another. Robert Mundell (Nobel Prize 1999) and Marcus Fleming added this openness to the model [2]. Just one more variable: ==the exchange rate==, the price of the country's currency in foreign currency.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.1: Key idea: if capital moves freely, the country's interest rate cannot stay away from the rest of the world's for long. If i rises, foreign money flows in to take advantage; if it falls, the money leaves.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.2: The basic model looks at a ==small open economy==: it has no weight on the rest of the world, whose income and interest rate are given. A third curve is added to IS and LM: balance-of-payments equilibrium (trade + capital).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.3: With floating exchange rates (the currency floats, like the euro against the dollar), the central bank keeps control of its currency, and ==monetary policy is even more effective than in a closed economy==: more money, rates fall, capital leaves, the currency depreciates, exports pick up and IS in turn shifts right. The more mobile capital is, the stronger the effect [2].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.4: Fiscal policy, on the other hand, works less the more mobile capital is: the stimulus raises rates, capital flows in, the currency appreciates, exports fall and cancel part of the stimulus (all of it if capital is perfectly mobile) [2].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.5: With fixed exchange rates (the currency is pegged to another), it is the opposite [2]. ==Monetary policy is useless in the long run==: if the central bank creates money, rates fall, capital leaves, the currency comes under attack, and to defend the peg it must sell its foreign-currency reserves, which withdraws as much money as it had created.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.6: ==Fiscal policy becomes effective, all the more so when capital is mobile==: the stimulus raises rates, capital comes in, the currency tends to appreciate; to hold the peg, the central bank buys foreign currency and creates money, like an involuntary policy mix. If capital is not very mobile, it is the opposite: imports win out, the currency is attacked, the central bank must withdraw money and crowding out worsens.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.7: The last tool under fixed exchange rates: ==devaluation==. It makes exports cheaper and should improve the trade balance, but first it worsens it (you pay more for what you already import): this is the ==J-curve==. It is all the less effective when capital is mobile.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.8: ==Large country, small country.== When a small country stimulates through money under fixed exchange rates, it has to defend its currency and gets nothing. When it is the dominant country (the United States), its monetary easing spreads to the others, who follow to keep their exchange rate: its policy becomes the world's.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.paragraphs.9: ==Monetary union (the euro area).== No more exchange rates between members, one central bank, one interest rate. If one country stimulates alone through spending, it raises the common rate: the crowding-out effect is shared by all its neighbours. Conversely, a common monetary policy acts the same way on everyone. And since a country no longer has to fear for its own currency, the temptation to let deficits run increases. Hence the rules of the Stability and Growth Pact: a public deficit of at most 3% of GDP and debt of at most 60%, with sanctions strengthened in 2011 [14].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.plain.title: France stimulates alone in 1981
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.plain.steps.0: The government hands out purchasing power: the French buy more [8].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.plain.steps.1: But a large share of these purchases are imported goods (cars, household appliances…): the stimulus also benefits foreign factories.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.plain.steps.2: France imports more than it exports: francs must be sold to pay in marks or dollars, and the franc is under pressure.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.plain.steps.3: Since the franc is pegged to the other European currencies, it has to be devalued, three times between 1981 and 1983 [8][9].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.plain.steps.4: In March 1983, the government changes course: this is the "turn to austerity" [10].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.example.title: Example: the French stimulus of 1981-1983
dossiers.is-lm.sections.8.example.text: In 1981, Pierre Mauroy's government boosted domestic demand [8]. Part of the stimulus went into imports, the external deficit widened, and the franc, pegged to the other European currencies, had to be devalued in October 1981 and twice more by March 1983 [8][9]. In March 1983, the government changed course: the "turn to austerity" [10]. The lesson of the open model: a country with fixed exchange rates that stimulates alone "leaks" through its imports; if capital does not come in to compensate, the currency is attacked and it must devalue or change policy.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.9.title: What is this model for?
dossiers.is-lm.sections.9.paragraphs.0: To reason quickly. Faced with a crisis, it gives the direction of the effects in two curves: what raises output, what raises rates, what cancels what.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.9.paragraphs.1: To understand the debates. Should the economy be stimulated through public spending or through money? The model shows that it depends on where rates stand, how open the country is and its exchange-rate regime.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.9.paragraphs.2: To read the news. When the ECB raises its rates, when a state passes a stimulus or austerity plan, you can ask yourself: which curve moves, in which direction, and what happens to output and rates?
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.title: The limits: a useful but simplified model
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.paragraphs.0: Prices are fixed. IS-LM describes the short run and ignores inflation: it does not say what happens to prices when output rises. For that, other models are needed (aggregate supply and demand).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.paragraphs.1: The liquidity trap. When rates are already at their floor, everyone expects them to rise again (and therefore bond prices to fall): people keep the extra money instead of buying bonds, and rates stop falling. LM is flat, and monetary policy no longer works in the model; fiscal policy, on the other hand, works fully. This was the situation in the United States after December 2008, when the Fed set its rate between 0 and 0.25% [5]: it had to rely on fiscal stimulus and other tools.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.paragraphs.2: Expectations. Households and firms react to what they expect: if people think today's stimulus will be paid for by taxes tomorrow, they may save instead of spending, and the effect is weaker. The model does not take these expectations into account (this is Robert Lucas's critique).
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.paragraphs.3: A simplified world. One output, one interest rate, no accumulating public debt, no banks that can refuse to lend: useful to understand the direction of the effects, not to forecast precise figures.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.plain.title: the liquidity trap, after 2008
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.plain.steps.0: In December 2008, the Fed has already set its rate between 0 and 0.25%: it can hardly lower it any more [5].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.plain.steps.1: Banks and households are afraid: even with cheap money, they do not borrow and keep their savings.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.plain.steps.2: Creating even more money changes almost nothing: that is the trap.
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.plain.steps.3: The state is what is left: in February 2009, the 787-billion-dollar stimulus plan takes over [3][4].
dossiers.is-lm.sections.10.diagram.steps: Rates are already at the floor: LM is flat where IS crosses it.
LM stretches to the right, but the point does not move: monetary policy no longer works.
IS moves right: output rises without rates moving. In the liquidity trap, fiscal stimulus is very effective.
dossiers.is-lm.forMe: When you read "the ECB raises its rates" or "the government announces a stimulus plan", you now know which curve moves: higher rates = more expensive loans and slower growth; public spending = more activity, but rates that may rise and a debt to pay.

dossiers.is-lm.quiz.0.q: In the IS-LM model, what does the IS curve represent?
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.0.explain: IS = goods market: the lower the interest rate, the more people invest and consume, the higher output is.
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.1.q: The state increases its spending. What happens in IS-LM?
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.1.explain: IS shifts right: output rises, but so does the interest rate, which holds back private investment (crowding out).
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.2.q: The central bank creates more money. What happens?
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.2.explain: LM shifts right: money is more plentiful and cheaper, rates fall and output rises.
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.3.options.1: The rise in rates caused by the stimulus, which reduces private investment
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.3.explain: Fiscal stimulus raises rates: part of private investment disappears, which reduces the effect of the stimulus.
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.4.q: In a liquidity trap (rates already at zero), which policy works best according to the model?
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.4.explain: Rates can no longer fall, so creating money is useless; public spending, however, raises output without raising rates.
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.5.q: With fixed exchange rates and highly mobile capital, which policy is effective according to Mundell-Fleming?
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.5.explain: The central bank must defend the peg and loses control of money; fiscal policy is effective, all the more so when capital is mobile.
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.6.q: For a monetarist, the LM curve is…
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.6.explain: Without speculative demand for money, the quantity of money sets output: LM is vertical, and fiscal stimulus only affects rates.
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.7.options.1: Households save debt-financed stimulus because they anticipate future taxes
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.7.explain: Households know today's debt will be paid by taxes tomorrow: they save, and the stimulus falls flat (under strong assumptions).
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.8.q: Which school dominated in the 1970s, facing stagflation?
dossiers.is-lm.quiz.8.explain: Unemployment and inflation at the same time: the Keynesian model was in trouble, and Friedman and the monetarists won the battle of ideas.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.title: The great schools of economics: classicals, Keynesians, monetarists…
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.hook: Faced with a crisis, two economists can give two opposite pieces of advice. Not because one of them is wrong, but because they do not look at the economy through the same glasses. Here are the great schools, their central idea and the era that made them win.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.tldr.0: Classical and neoclassical economists trust markets: left free, they return to equilibrium, and the state should stay in the background [1][2].
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.tldr.1: Keynes responds to the crisis of the 1930s: demand can remain too weak, unemployment can last, and the state must stimulate [3].
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.tldr.2: The monetarists (Friedman) and then the new classicals (Lucas) take over in the 1970s-1980s: watch money, distrust stimulus [5][6].
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.tldr.3: Each school was born from a crisis that the previous one explained poorly: the question to ask is not "who is right?" but "which glasses for which moment?".
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.0.t: The classicals: the market balances itself
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.0.p: In 1776, the Scot Adam Smith published "The Wealth of Nations": each person, by pursuing their own interest, unintentionally contributes to the wealth of all, as if guided by an "invisible hand" [1]. In 1817 David Ricardo added comparative advantage, which justifies free trade.

The central idea: ==markets adjust==. If wages are too high, they fall until everyone finds a job. According to "Say's law" (Jean-Baptiste Say), supply creates its own demand: there can be no lasting shortage of demand.
Money is only a "veil": it does not change real output, only prices. The state has limited functions: justice, defence, some infrastructure.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.0.e: Faced with a crisis, the classical advice
Force nothing: let prices and wages fall, and the economy will return to full employment on its own. Balance the state budget.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.1.t: The neoclassicals: economics put into equations
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.1.p: In the 1870s, Léon Walras, William Jevons and Carl Menger changed the method: the value of a good comes from its utility to the buyer, and reasoning is done "at the margin" (what one more unit brings) [2]. Walras built general equilibrium: all markets balance at the same time.
Their legacy is immense: supply and demand, adjusting prices, perfect competition. It is still the basis of most economics textbooks.
Their view of crises remains that of the classicals: lasting unemployment comes from whatever prevents prices from adjusting (minimum wages, unions, regulations).
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.2.t: Keynes: what if the market did not recover on its own?
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.2.p: The 1929 crisis drags on and unemployment stays massive for years: markets do not recover. In 1936, John Maynard Keynes published "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money" [3].

His idea: ==demand determines output==. If households and firms fear the future, they spend less, firms produce less and hire less, and unemployment can last: it is an ==underemployment equilibrium==. Cutting wages can even make things worse, because workers consume less.
The remedy: ==the state stimulates== demand (public spending, tax cuts), even if that means running a deficit during the crisis. Money matters too, but it can run into the liquidity trap.
Keynes also stresses uncertainty and investors' "animal spirits": investment depends on confidence, not only on the interest rate.
the vicious circle of the Great Depression
After the 1929 crash, households are afraid and spend less.
Factories sell less and lay people off.
The unemployed spend even less: sales fall again, other factories lay people off.
Cutting wages does not help: workers buy even less.
For Keynes, someone has to spend in place of households: the state.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.2.d: Demand is too weak: the economy is stuck at point E, with unemployment.
Public spending pushes IS to the right: output goes back up. This is the Keynesian answer.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.2.e: Faced with a crisis, the Keynesian advice
Stimulate: the state spends (major works, support) and accepts a deficit until private demand picks up. The 2009 American plan is an example (see the IS-LM course).
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.3.t: The synthesis: Keynes in the short run, the classicals in the long run
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.3.p: After the war, economists such as John Hicks (the IS-LM model, 1937) and Paul Samuelson reconciled the two camps: in the short run, prices are rigid and Keynes is right; in the long run, prices adjust and the neoclassicals are right [4].

This was the Keynesian golden age of the 1950s-1960s: strong growth, full employment, and states steering the economy with the budget and money. The Phillips curve seemed to offer a choice: a bit more inflation for a bit less unemployment.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.4.p: In the 1970s, everything went haywire: stagflation (stagnation + inflation) combined unemployment and inflation, which the Phillips curve said was impossible. Milton Friedman, of the University of Chicago, had warned of it [5].

His ideas: ==inflation is first and foremost a monetary phenomenon== (too much money chasing too few goods); in the long run, there is a =="natural" rate of unemployment== that cannot be lowered durably by creating inflation; fiscal stimulus crowds out private investment.
His advice: a ==simple rule==, growing the money supply at the same pace as the economy, rather than case-by-case stimulus. Friedman received the Nobel Prize in 1976 [5].
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.4.d: LM is vertical: the quantity of money sets output.
IS moves right, but only rates rise: fiscal stimulus is useless.
Output rises in the short run; in the long run, only prices rise.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.4.e: Faced with a crisis, the monetarist advice
Do not multiply fiscal stimulus packages; stabilise money growth and fight inflation first. In the early 1980s, Paul Volcker's Fed tightened money to break American inflation (see the IS-LM course).
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.5.p: Robert Lucas (Nobel Prize 1995) went further with ==rational expectations==: households and firms use all available information and are not fooled for long [6]. If the state announces a stimulus, they anticipate its effects (inflation, future taxes) and adjust their behaviour: the stimulus loses its effect.
Robert Barro derived ==Ricardian equivalence== from it (1974): debt-financed stimulus is saved by households, who foresee tomorrow's taxes [7].
Practical consequences: ==rules rather than surprises==, independent and credible central banks, tasked first with price stability. This is the model of the ECB, created in 1998.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.6.t: The new Keynesians: prices do not adjust that fast
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.6.p: Since the 1980s, another family has taken up the tools of the new classicals (rational expectations, rigorous calculations) but kept Keynes's intuition: ==prices and wages are sticky==. Changing prices is costly (catalogues, contracts, negotiations), and information is imperfect: a used-car seller knows more than the buyer, as George Akerlof (Nobel Prize 2001) showed [8].
The result: in the short run, economic policy can help. Today it is the framework most used by central banks, which mix it with ideas from the other schools.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.7.t: And the others: Austrians, Marxists, post-Keynesians…
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.7.p: ==The Austrian school== (Friedrich Hayek, Nobel Prize 1974) is even more wary of the state than the classicals: prices convey information that no planner can gather, and crises come from credit that is too easy [9].
==Marxists== see capitalism as a conflict between those who own capital and those who sell their labour, with crises that recur by nature.
==Post-Keynesians== extend Keynes's radical uncertainty and stress the fragility of finance and the role of money created by banks.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.8.t: What to remember: which glasses for which moment?
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.8.p: Each school was born from a crisis that the previous one explained poorly: Keynes after 1929, the monetarists after the stagflation of the 1970s, the return of Keynesian ideas after 2008, when rates fell to zero.

None is right everywhere and always. When the problem is collapsed demand, Keynesian glasses help; when it is inflation, monetarist glasses; when economic policy is unpredictable, those of the new classicals.
In a debate, ask yourself: ==which school is this person speaking from, and what situation are we in?== That is often where the disagreement lies.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.forMe: When one politician says "we need a stimulus" and another answers "we need to cut the deficit", you can recognise their schools: the first reasons as a Keynesian, the second as a classical or a monetarist. And you can ask yourself which one best fits the situation of the moment.

dossiers.ecoles-economiques.figures.3.la: Nobel Prize for Robert Lucas and rational expectations
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.0.expla: For the classicals, there can be no lasting shortage of demand: what is produced ends up being sold.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.1.q: Which crisis gave birth to Keynes's thinking?
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.1.optio: The 1929 crisis and the Great Depression
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.1.expla: The massive and lasting unemployment of the 1930s contradicted the idea that markets recover on their own; the "General Theory" came out in 1936.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.2.q: For Milton Friedman, inflation is first and foremost…
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.2.expla: Too much money chasing too few goods: for the monetarists, the quantity of money explains inflation.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.3.optio: People use all the information and are not fooled for long by economic policy
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.3.expla: If people anticipate the effects of a stimulus, it loses much of its effectiveness: hence the preference for stable rules.
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.4.q: What sets the new Keynesians apart?
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.4.optio: They think prices and wages are sticky in the short run
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.quiz.4.expla: They keep modern tools but add rigidities: in the short run, economic policy can help.
dossiers.eurodollars.title: Eurodollars: the dollars that live outside the United States
dossiers.eurodollars.hook: Trillions of dollars circulate in banks in London, Tokyo or Singapore, far from the Fed's control. They were born of the Cold War, and in every major crisis it is the Fed that has to come to their rescue.
dossiers.eurodollars.tldr.0: A eurodollar is simply a dollar deposited in a bank outside the United States. It has nothing to do with the euro: the word was coined long before [1][2].
dossiers.eurodollars.tldr.1: The market was born in the mid-1950s, when Soviet banks placed their dollars in London and Paris for fear they would be seized in the United States [1].
dossiers.eurodollars.tldr.2: It grew because it escaped American rules (interest-rate ceilings, reserve requirements): at the end of 2019, non-US banks owed around 13 trillion dollars [1][3].
dossiers.eurodollars.tldr.3: When these dollars run short, as in 2008 and 2020, the Fed lends dollars to other central banks: the "swap lines" [4][5].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.0.title: A dollar… that is not in the United States
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.0.paragrap: When a French company deposits dollars in a bank in Paris, or a London bank lends dollars to a Brazilian company, we speak of ==eurodollars==: dollars deposited or lent ==outside the United States== [2].

The prefix "euro" comes from the fact that the first ones were in Europe, mainly in London. It stuck, even for dollars in Tokyo or Singapore, and has no link with the European currency created much later [2].

These dollars are not banknotes hidden in a safe: they are ==dollar debts recorded on the balance sheets of foreign banks==. The London bank owes dollars to its client, and it lends those dollars to others.
An Indonesian airline buys planes paid for in dollars. It borrows these dollars from a bank in Singapore, which itself borrowed them from a fund or another bank. None of these dollars passes through an American bank: it is a eurodollar circuit.
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.1.title: Born of the Cold War
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.1.paragrap: In the mid-1950s, the Soviet Union needed dollars to trade, but its banks feared the American government would seize their assets deposited in the United States. So they placed them in banks in London and Paris [1].
London banks then discovered that they could accept and lend dollars out of reach of American rules. The market took off, with the City as its centre [1][2].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.2.title: Why it grew so much
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.2.paragrap: In the United States, ==Regulation Q== capped the interest rates banks could pay on deposits, and banks had to hold reserve requirements. In London, none of that: banks could pay more on dollar deposits and lend more cheaply [1][2].
American banks themselves joined in: in 1969, the Fed allowed them to use "shell" branches in the Bahamas (Nassau) to take part in the market without opening an office in London [1].

Competition from this free market ended up changing American banking itself, up to the end of interest-rate ceilings on deposits [1]. With the oil shock, the dollars of producing countries ("petrodollars") also swelled this circuit.
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.3.title: Today: a giant that no one really controls
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.3.paragrap: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the "central banks' bank", measures this market through the dollar debts of banks located outside the United States [3].

At the end of 2019, banks headquartered outside the United States owed around ==13 trillion dollars==, almost as much as before the 2008 crisis, and most of it was booked outside American territory [3].

This is one reason for the dollar's power: the whole world borrows, trades and goes into debt in dollars, even without going through America (see the course on the dollar). But it is also a weakness: the Fed creates dollars, not the banks of London or Tokyo.
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.4.title: When dollars run short: the "swap lines"
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.4.paragrap: A European bank that has lent dollars long-term and funded itself in dollars short-term is in danger if no one wants to lend it dollars any more. It cannot create them: only the Fed can.

That is what happened in 2008. As early as 12 December 2007, the Fed opened ==swap lines== with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank: it lent them dollars against their currency, and they re-lent them to their banks [4]. The network grew to 14 central banks, and in December 2008 more than 580 billion dollars were lent, over 25% of the Fed's balance sheet [4].
In 2020, with Covid, the same mechanism was revived: use of the swap lines reached 449 billion dollars in May [5].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.4.plain.st: A European bank has lent dollars to companies for several years, funding itself overnight from other banks.
Lehman Brothers goes bankrupt: no one trusts anyone any more, and the other banks stop lending it dollars.
The ECB cannot help it directly: it creates euros, not dollars.
The Fed lends dollars to the ECB against euros (a swap line), and the ECB re-lends them to its banks [4].
The banks hold on: the Fed acted as firefighter for the whole dollar system, not just for America.
The Fed is not just the central bank of the United States: in a crisis, it becomes the lender of last resort for the whole dollar system. Countries with a swap line with it are protected; the others have to draw on their reserves or turn to the IMF.
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.5.title: Uses and limits
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.5.paragrap: ==Useful==: the eurodollar market lets world trade finance itself in the currency it uses, often at lower rates, all over the world.
==Risky==: it partly escapes the authorities, can swell very quickly, and ultimately relies on the Fed's goodwill. A dollar liquidity crisis in London or Tokyo can spread to the whole planet.
==Geopolitical==: access to dollars becomes a lever. Being cut off from the dollar circuit, as with sanctions, can paralyse a country (see the course on sanctions).
dossiers.eurodollars.forMe: If your bank, your company or your country needs dollars, it depends on this global market and therefore, in a crisis, on the Fed's decisions. That is why an American banking crisis can shake European or Asian markets.

glossary.politique-budgetaire.def: Using public spending and taxes to influence activity: spending more or cutting taxes to stimulate, the opposite to slow down (austerity).
glossary.politique-budgetaire.example: A stimulus plan that funds public works.
glossary.politique-monetaire.def: Action by the central bank on the quantity of money and interest rates to support activity or curb inflation.
glossary.politique-monetaire.example: The ECB raising or lowering its policy rates.
glossary.multiplicateur.def: Public spending becomes someone's income, who spends part of it, which becomes someone else's income… Final output can rise by more than the initial spending.
glossary.multiplicateur.example: 10 billion spent can raise output by more than 10 billion.
glossary.effet-eviction.def: A fiscal stimulus first raises output (income effect, the multiplier), then the interest rate rises and part of private investment disappears: this is crowding out, the gap between the increase "at an unchanged rate" and the final increase.
glossary.effet-eviction.example: The state borrows heavily, rates rise, a company gives up building a factory.
glossary.piege-liquidite.def: A situation where interest rates are already at their lowest: creating more money no longer brings them down, and monetary policy loses its effect.
glossary.piege-liquidite.example: The United States after 2008, with the Fed's rate close to zero.

culture.reaganomics.title: Reaganomics: the revolution that set out to "free" the American economy
culture.reaganomics.hook: 1980: American prices are rising by more than 13% a year, unemployment is climbing, and a former actor promises to change everything by cutting taxes. Eight years later, inflation has been tamed and growth is back… and the debt has tripled. A look back at the economic experiment that still divides economists.
culture.reaganomics.tldr.0: Reaganomics is the economic policy of Ronald Reagan (1981-1989), built on ==four pillars==: cutting taxes, curbing public spending, deregulating and breaking inflation with tight money [1].
culture.reaganomics.tldr.1: It relies on ==supply-side economics==: by cutting taxes, people would be encouraged to work, save and invest, to the point that state revenue might even rise (the "Laffer curve") [1][8].
culture.reaganomics.tldr.2: Results: inflation fell from about 13.5% in 1980 to 4.1% in 1988 and growth came back strongly, but at the cost of a brutal recession in 1981-1982 (10.8% unemployment) [3][14].
culture.reaganomics.tldr.3: The downside: rearmament and tax cuts widened deficits, ==federal debt went from 995 billion to 2,900 billion dollars==, the dollar soared and the trade deficit with it [5][11].

culture.reaganomics.timeline.1.text: Inflation around 13.5%: Reagan is elected against Jimmy Carter [14].

culture.reaganomics.sections.0.title: "Government is not the solution, it is the problem"
culture.reaganomics.sections.0.quote: In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem. Ronald Reagan, 20 January 1981 [12].
culture.reaganomics.sections.0.paragraph: Washington, 20 January 1981. On the steps of the Capitol, Ronald Reagan, 69, a former Hollywood actor and former governor of California, takes the oath. His inaugural address contains a sentence that sums up an entire programme: =="government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem"== [12].

The country he inherits is in bad shape. Prices rose by about 13% in 1979, then again at the same pace in 1980 [3][14]. To break this inflation, Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve pushed its policy rate up to a record level of about 20% [3]. Borrowing to buy a house or a car becomes almost impossible. This is ==stagflation==: a stagnating economy and soaring prices at the same time, which the Keynesian recipes of the 1960s can no longer cure (see our course on the schools of economics).

Reagan arrives with a simple diagnosis: the state takes too much, spends too much and regulates too much. Those who produce must be freed. This programme will get a name, mocking at first and then embraced: ==Reaganomics==.
culture.reaganomics.sections.1.title: A curve scribbled on a napkin
culture.reaganomics.sections.1.quote: At 0% tax, the state earns nothing. At 100%, no one works, and it earns nothing either.
culture.reaganomics.sections.1.paragraph: The story has become a legend. In 1974, in a Washington restaurant, the Two Continents, the economist Arthur Laffer explains a simple idea to White House advisers, including Dick Cheney, and draws it [8]. The "Laffer napkin" is now on display at the Smithsonian… even though its authenticity is disputed: the museum's is made of cloth and dated September 1974, whereas the dinner reportedly took place after the November elections [8].

The idea, however, is clear. If tax is at 0%, the state collects nothing. If it is at 100%, no one has any interest in working or declaring income: the state collects nothing either. In between, there is a rate that brings in the most. And if tax is already very high, ==cutting it could bring in more money==, because people would work and invest more and cheat less. This is the Laffer curve, popularised in 1978 by the journalist Jude Wanniski [8].

Behind it, a whole school: ==supply-side economics==. Instead of boosting demand like Keynes (the state spends, households consume), it aims to stimulate supply: cutting taxes and rules so that firms produce and invest more. The decisive question, which the curve does not settle, is ==where the United States really stood on the curve in 1981==: high enough for a tax cut to pay for itself, or not?
culture.reaganomics.sections.1.box.label: How it works
culture.reaganomics.sections.1.box.title: Demand or supply: two ways to stimulate
Demand-side stimulus (Keynes): the state spends or cuts taxes for households that consume; consumption keeps firms running.

Supply-side stimulus (Reagan): taxes are cut mainly on high incomes, savings and companies, and rules are relaxed; the hope is that investment and work will increase, and that the gains will "trickle down" to everyone.
culture.reaganomics.sections.2.title: The four pillars
culture.reaganomics.sections.2.quote: Less tax, less spending, fewer rules, less inflation.
culture.reaganomics.sections.2.paragraph: Reaganomics rests on four pillars: ==slowing the growth of public spending, cutting tax rates, easing regulation, and restraining the money supply to break inflation== [1].

The first act comes quickly. On 13 August 1981, Reagan signs the Economic Recovery Tax Act (ERTA) [2]. The top income tax rate falls from 70% to 50%, the lowest from 14% to 11%, with cuts phased in over three years and incentives for business investment [2].

Spending, for its part, is distributed very unevenly. Reagan wants to cut social programmes and the state's role in the economy, but at the same time he launches a ==vast rearmament== against the Soviet Union [5]. Less tax, more defence: the budget equation only holds if growth and the Laffer curve work miracles.

Deregulation affects several sectors of the economy [1]. And the fourth pillar, money, is not in the president's hands but in those of the independent Fed: Paul Volcker will take care of it, in his own way.
culture.reaganomics.sections.3.title: The shock therapy: Volcker and the 1981-1982 recession
culture.reaganomics.sections.3.quote: To break inflation, growth had to be broken.
culture.reaganomics.sections.3.paragraph: Paul Volcker, appointed by Carter in 1979, keeps interest rates extremely high: the Fed's rate stays above 14% from February to June 1982 [13]. The effect is the one predicted by the IS-LM model (see our course): money becomes scarce, credit becomes prohibitively expensive, home and car purchases collapse, firms invest less.
The price is terrible. The economy plunges into the worst recession since the Great Depression: unemployment reaches ==10.8% in November and December 1982== [3].

Reagan nevertheless backs Volcker. And the bet eventually pays off on inflation: it falls to 4.1% in 1988, against about 13.5% in 1980 [14]. Many economists in fact credit this victory first to the Fed, more than to the tax cuts.
culture.reaganomics.sections.3.box.label: The forgotten detail
culture.reaganomics.sections.3.box.title: The 11,000 air traffic controllers
On 3 August 1981, some 13,000 federal air traffic controllers go on strike over pay and working conditions, even though strikes are forbidden for federal employees [6]. Reagan gives them 48 hours to return to work, then fires the 11,345 who refuse, with a lifetime ban on working for the federal government [6]. The union is decertified in October [6].
The message carries far beyond the skies: across the country, unions lose influence and wage increases slow down. Bill Clinton will lift the ban in 1993 [7].
culture.reaganomics.sections.4.title: The balancing act: rearmament, deficits and a strong dollar
culture.reaganomics.sections.4.quote: A state that cuts taxes and raises spending has to borrow somewhere.
culture.reaganomics.sections.4.paragraph: Growth returns, but revenue does not live up to the promises of the Laffer curve, and military spending explodes. Deficits widen. During Reagan's eight years, ==gross federal debt rises from 995 billion to 2,900 billion dollars== [5].

Reagan has to correct course. As early as 1982, he signs a tax increase, the Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act (TEFRA), which he defends on television on 16 August, insisting that he is not abandoning his policy [10]. Other increases will follow. Reaganomics was therefore never one continuous tax cut.

The mix is explosive: ==a very expansionary budget (IS to the right) and very tight money (LM to the left)==. The result, exactly as the diagram predicts: very high interest rates. These rates attract capital from all over the world, which buys American debt: ==the dollar soars==. American goods become too expensive abroad, cheap imports flood the country, and a ==trade deficit== opens up alongside the budget deficit: these are the "twin deficits" [11].

In September 1985, the United States and four other major economies meet at the Plaza Hotel in New York and agree to bring the dollar down: this is the Plaza Accord [11]. Japan, whose currency appreciates sharply, will pay the price with a bubble followed by a long crisis [11].
culture.reaganomics.sections.4.box.label: The course to understand
culture.reaganomics.sections.4.box.title: Crowding out, 1980s version
This is the textbook case from the IS-LM course: a fiscal stimulus raises rates, and part of private activity is crowded out.

Here, crowding out works through two channels: rates (investment and housing suffer) and the exchange rate (the strong dollar crowds out exports). This is exactly Mundell-Fleming's prediction for a country with floating exchange rates.
culture.reaganomics.sections.5.title: The world pays the bill too
culture.reaganomics.sections.5.quote: When American rates rise, it is not only America that tightens its belt.
culture.reaganomics.sections.5.paragraph: Reaganomics does not stop at the borders of the United States. The dollar is the currency in which the world borrows, trades and sells its oil (see our article on the petrodollar). When American rates climb to record levels, countries indebted in dollars also choke.

In the 1970s, Latin American countries borrowed heavily from American banks, often at variable rates [16]. When Volcker's Fed sends the cost of money soaring, their interest payments follow. In August 1982, Mexico's finance minister warns the Fed, the Treasury and the IMF: Mexico can no longer pay [17]. The Latin American debt held by the nine largest American banks then amounts to 176% of their capital [17]. For Latin America, the 1980s become the "lost decade" [16].

Europe feels the shock differently. A strong dollar and very high American rates draw capital to New York and force other countries to keep rates high to defend their currencies. France in 1981, stimulating alone while America tightens the screws, experiences this first-hand: franc devaluations, then the turn to austerity in 1983 (see our IS-LM course).

This is the other face of the American "privilege": ==a decision taken in Washington for American inflation is transmitted to the whole world==, through rates and through the dollar. The 1985 Plaza Accord, which organised the dollar's decline with Japan, Germany, France and the United Kingdom, shows that in the end even Washington had to take its partners into account [11].
culture.reaganomics.sections.6.title: "Morning in America": the return of growth
culture.reaganomics.sections.6.quote: In 1984, America feels strong again, and says so at the ballot box.
culture.reaganomics.sections.6.paragraph: From 1983, the economy rebounds strongly. Growth reaches ==7.3% in 1984==, and Reagan is triumphantly re-elected the same year [15]. Inflation remains contained [14].

In 1986, Reagan obtains a second major tax reform, passed with the Democrats: the Tax Reform Act lowers the top rate from 50% to 28%, simplifies the tax code and reduces the number of brackets, while eliminating many loopholes [1]. It is often cited as a model of bipartisan reform.

For its supporters, Reaganomics ended stagflation, revived entrepreneurship and paved the way for the long growth of the following decades, while contributing, through the arms race, to the exhaustion of the Soviet Union.
culture.reaganomics.sections.7.title: The case against: trickle-down, inequality and debt
culture.reaganomics.sections.7.quote: "It's kind of hard to sell 'trickle down'": the admission of budget director David Stockman in 1981 [9].
culture.reaganomics.sections.7.paragraph: The criticism is just as old. In December 1981, The Atlantic magazine published long interviews with David Stockman, Reagan's young budget director. In them he acknowledged that the tax cut was, in his words, a "Trojan horse" to bring down the top rate, and that supply-side economics was basically a "trickle-down" theory [9]. The article nearly cost him his job [9].

==Trickle-down== is the idea that gains granted to the richest and to companies end up benefiting everyone, through investment and jobs. Its critics reply that ==income inequality widened== in the United States in the 1980s, and that union power declined sharply [15].

Then there is the debt. The Laffer curve promised that tax cuts would partly pay for themselves: most economists believe they did not, since the debt tripled [5]. Reagan's defenders reply that rearmament, not tax cuts, explains most of the deficits, and that victory over inflation was worth the price.
culture.reaganomics.sections.7.box.label: Head to head
culture.reaganomics.sections.7.box.title: Two readings of the same record
For: the end of stagflation, inflation brought down to 4.1% in 1988, strong growth from 1983, simpler taxes, and an America that emerged stronger from the Cold War [14][15].
Against: a very harsh recession in 1982, a tripled debt, twin deficits, rising inequality and weakened unions [3][5][11]. And a victory over inflation owed mainly to the Fed.
culture.reaganomics.sections.8.title: What remains of it
culture.reaganomics.sections.8.quote: Forty years on, every tax debate replays a bit of 1981.
culture.reaganomics.sections.8.paragraph: Reaganomics profoundly changed the economic debate. Together with Margaret Thatcher in the United Kingdom at the same time, it embodies the great liberal turn of the 1980s: less state, more market, central banks that make inflation their priority.

Its ideas return with every new tax cut in the United States, with the same arguments on both sides: stimulating supply, or deepening debt and inequality? The Laffer curve itself commands consensus on the principle (too much tax kills tax), much less on the level where that "too much" begins.

For an economics student, it is a real-life laboratory: an extreme policy mix (expansionary budget, tight money), record rates, a strong dollar and twin deficits, exactly what the IS-LM and Mundell-Fleming models predict. And for a citizen, a lesson: ==an economic policy should be judged on all its effects, not only on the ones that were promised==.

culture.petrodollar.title: The petrodollar: how Washington made oil the dollar's ally
culture.petrodollar.hook: On an American cruiser anchored in the middle of the Suez Canal, an ailing president and a desert king seal an unlikely friendship. Thirty years later, it will make the dollar the currency of oil, and the United States the policeman of the Gulf. The story of a system that no one ever signed, but that everyone uses.
culture.petrodollar.tldr.0: Oil is paid for in dollars almost everywhere: to buy it, the whole world must first obtain dollars, and producing countries reinvest a large part of their earnings in America [7].
culture.petrodollar.tldr.1: The system was born in the 1970s: the dollar lost its link to gold (1971), the price of oil quadrupled (1973-1974), and ==Washington struck a security-for-dollars partnership with Saudi Arabia== [3][4][5][6].
culture.petrodollar.tldr.2: The United States gained easy financing for its deficits and a financial weapon; it took on the price: ==casting itself as the armed protector of the Gulf==, from the Carter Doctrine (1980) to the Gulf War (1991) [10][12].
culture.petrodollar.tldr.3: The recycling of these dollars also had its victims: lent to Latin America, they fed the 1982 debt crisis [8][9]. And no, the petrodollar did not "expire" in 2024 [13][14].
