culture.petrodollar.sections.0.title: A king, a president and a cruiser
culture.petrodollar.sections.0.quote: That day, no one talks about dollars. They talk about security, oil and Palestine.
culture.petrodollar.sections.0.paragraph: February 1945. The war is not over, and Franklin D. Roosevelt is returning exhausted from the Yalta conference, where he has just redrawn the post-war world with Churchill and Stalin. On the way back, he makes a detour: from 12 to 14 February, the cruiser USS Quincy drops anchor in the Great Bitter Lake, in the middle of the Suez Canal [1][2]. An American destroyer has gone to Jeddah to fetch a distinguished guest: Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, founder of the kingdom of Saudi Arabia [1].

The two men do not speak the same language; a Marine colonel, William Eddy, acts as interpreter [1]. The conversation is dominated by a disagreement: the future of Palestine, where Roosevelt supports the idea of a Jewish homeland that the king rejects [2]. Yet this meeting is often presented as the birth certificate of an alliance that has lasted 80 years [2].

Why? Because their interests intersect. The United States already knows that oil will be the lifeblood of the post-war economy, and that Saudi soil is full of it. The kingdom, for its part, is young, vast, sparsely populated and surrounded by powerful neighbours: it needs a distant protector, strong enough to deter, far enough away not to colonise. ==The underlying bargain is set: oil for security.== The dollar will come later.
culture.petrodollar.sections.0.box.label: The forgotten detail
culture.petrodollar.sections.0.box.title: A meeting in the middle of the Suez Canal
culture.petrodollar.sections.0.box.text: The Quincy is not at a quay: it is anchored in the Great Bitter Lake, a widening of the Suez Canal. The king came by sea from Jeddah, aboard the destroyer USS Murphy, sent especially for him [1].
culture.petrodollar.sections.1.title: 1971: the dollar without gold
culture.petrodollar.sections.1.quote: The dollar is no longer worth gold. It is only worth what the world is willing to make of it.
culture.petrodollar.sections.1.paragraph: Since 1944 and the Bretton Woods agreements, the dollar has been at the centre of the monetary system: other currencies are pegged to it, and foreign central banks can exchange their dollars for gold at a fixed price. The dollar is "as good as gold".

But at the end of the 1960s, the United States has issued far more dollars than it has gold to back them: the Vietnam War and social programmes are expensive, and foreigners are starting to demand gold. On 15 August 1971, Richard Nixon closes the "gold window": dollars are no longer convertible [3].
The shock is immense. ==Why would the world keep dollars that are backed by nothing but American power?== That is precisely the question oil will answer.
culture.petrodollar.sections.2.title: 1973-1974: the shock, then the understanding
culture.petrodollar.sections.2.quote: The Gulf countries suddenly have more dollars than they can spend. Washington knows exactly where to place them.
culture.petrodollar.sections.2.paragraph: In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil producers declare an embargo against countries that support Israel, including the United States. The price of a barrel quadruples [4]. Queues at American petrol stations become the image of the decade.

For Washington, it is a double alarm: strategic (oil can become a weapon) and financial (mountains of dollars are piling up in the Gulf's coffers). The response is diplomatic before it is monetary. On 8 June 1974, Secretary of State Henry Kissinger and Crown Prince Fahd announce the creation of joint commissions: one for economic cooperation, the other for security [5].

In July 1974, Treasury Secretary William Simon, a former bond trader, flies to Saudi Arabia. According to a Bloomberg investigation published in 2016, the logic is as follows: the United States buys Saudi oil and provides military aid and equipment; in return, the kingdom reinvests billions of its oil revenues in American Treasury bonds, which helps finance Washington's spending [6].

The Treasury sets up tailor-made treatment: Saudi purchases go through "add-ons" outside the usual auctions, and they are excluded from the detailed country-by-country statistics published by the administration [6]. In 1977, Saudi Arabia holds about 20% of all American Treasury bonds held abroad [6].
culture.petrodollar.sections.2.box.label: True or false?
culture.petrodollar.sections.2.box.title: Was a "petrodollar agreement" signed?
No known official document obliges Saudi Arabia to sell its oil only in dollars [7][13]. The 1974 texts concern economic and military cooperation [5].
The petrodollar is therefore a de facto arrangement, carried by common interests, far more than a contract. That is also what made it solid: you cannot "terminate" what was never signed.
culture.petrodollar.sections.3.title: How the dollar pump works
culture.petrodollar.sections.3.quote: A tanker leaves the Gulf for Yokohama. The oil goes to Japan, the dollars head back to New York.
culture.petrodollar.sections.3.paragraph: To understand the system, let's follow a single tanker. A Japanese refinery buys a cargo of Saudi crude. The price is set in dollars: before paying, it must sell yen and buy dollars on the foreign exchange market. Multiply this operation by every importer on the planet, from India to France: ==the whole world needs dollars continuously, simply to keep its cars and factories running== [7].

On the Saudi side, dollars pile up. The kingdom spends some of them (salaries, infrastructure, imports), but for a long time oil revenue far exceeds what it can absorb. The rest has to be invested, and the safest, most liquid and largest investment in the world is American government debt. That is exactly what Simon's 1974 mission organised [6].

The loop closes: the dollars that left the United States to pay for oil come back as loans to the American state. Washington can thus finance its deficits without raising its interest rates as much as another country would. And part of these dollars is also used to buy American weapons and expertise: the 1974 economic commission mobilises American experts on Saudi projects, financed by the kingdom itself [5].
culture.petrodollar.sections.3.box.label: How it works
culture.petrodollar.sections.3.box.title: The loop in four steps
1. An importing country buys dollars to pay for its oil.
2. The producing country collects these dollars.
3. It reinvests a large share in American debt, bank deposits and purchases of American weapons or services [5][6].
4. These dollars come back to finance the American economy and state: the pump starts another round.
culture.petrodollar.sections.4.title: Why Washington cared so much
culture.petrodollar.sections.4.quote: A country whose currency is in demand everywhere can borrow in its own currency, cheaply, almost without limit.
culture.petrodollar.sections.4.paragraph: Seen from Washington, the arrangement solves several problems at once. First, ==it keeps the dollar at the centre of the world== despite the end of gold: since oil is bought in dollars, every importing country, from Japan to France, permanently needs dollars [7].

Next, ==it finances America==. The dollars paid for oil largely return to the United States in the form of purchases of public debt: that is what Simon came to get in 1974 [6]. A state whose debt is always in demand borrows more cheaply and more easily than others; this is part of what the French minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing called, as early as the 1960s, the dollar's "exorbitant privilege".

Finally, ==it anchors the Gulf in the Western camp== in the middle of the Cold War. Every dollar invested in New York, every arms contract, every American engineer in the oil fields makes the kingdom a little more dependent on Washington, and a little less tempted by Moscow.

Saudi leaders also find it worthwhile: a safe, liquid investment for gigantic revenues and, above all, the guarantee that in the event of a threat the world's leading army will be on their side. It is this balance that explains the system's longevity, far more than any unilateral pressure.
culture.petrodollar.sections.5.title: The policeman of the Gulf
culture.petrodollar.sections.5.quote: An attempt by any outside force to gain control of the Persian Gulf region will be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the United States. Jimmy Carter, 23 January 1980 [10].
culture.petrodollar.sections.5.paragraph: The promise of protection is about to become a doctrine. In December 1979, the Soviet Union invades Afghanistan, a few hundred kilometres from the Strait of Hormuz. On 23 January 1980, in his State of the Union address, Jimmy Carter warns: the United States will repel any attempt by an outside power to control the region, ==including by military force== [10]. This is the Carter Doctrine.

For the first time, Washington openly declares that the security of the Gulf's oil flows is one of its vital interests. Oil, the dollar and the American military now form a single whole: the United States protects the region the barrels come from, the barrels are sold in dollars, and the dollars come back to finance America, including its army.

The doctrine is put to the test in August 1990, when Saddam Hussein's Iraq invades Kuwait. In January 1991, a coalition of several dozen countries led by the United States launches Operation Desert Storm and drives out the Iraqi army [12]. Washington then clearly casts itself as the ==policeman of the Gulf==, and more broadly as the guarantor of the post-Cold War international order.

This role has its defenders, who see it as the condition for a stable global supply that also benefits Europe and Asia, and its critics, who see it as the armed defence of American economic interests. Both readings rest on the same facts: the American military presence in the Gulf is inseparable from the oil found there.
culture.petrodollar.sections.5.box.label: The disputed case
culture.petrodollar.sections.5.box.title: Iraq, the euro and 2003
In November 2000, Iraq obtained from the UN that its oil sold under the "oil for food" programme be paid for in euros, a move presented as a challenge to Washington's sanctions policy [11]. The White House replied at the time that the currency mattered little [11].

Some authors link this choice to the invasion of Iraq in 2003. That is a thesis, not an established fact: the official reasons and the debates of the time concerned weapons of mass destruction and terrorism. Geonomix mentions it because it circulates widely, not because it is proven.
culture.petrodollar.sections.6.title: The dollar weapon
culture.petrodollar.sections.6.quote: When the world pays in dollars, the world goes, one way or another, through American banks.
culture.petrodollar.sections.6.paragraph: The petrodollar has a consequence less visible than aircraft carriers, but just as powerful. Since a large part of world trade, starting with oil, is settled in dollars, most major international payments pass at some point through American banks or through banks that cannot do without access to the American market. ==This is what gives American sanctions their global reach.==

France learned this the hard way. In 2014, the bank BNP Paribas agreed to plead guilty before American courts and to pay 8.9 billion dollars for routing dollar payments linked to countries under American sanctions, notably Sudan, Iran and Cuba [17]. A European bank, sanctioned by Washington, for operations outside the United States: it is the dollar that gives this jurisdiction.

In 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, the United States, the European Union and their allies froze the Russian central bank's reserves held with them and excluded several Russian banks from SWIFT, the messaging system for international transfers [16]. For many countries, this was a signal: reserves in dollars or euros can be blocked overnight.

Seen from Washington, it is a foreign-policy instrument without soldiers, one that enforces rules without war. Seen from Beijing, Moscow or Tehran, it is a reason to look for alternatives. ==The policeman's role now runs as much through banks as through military bases.==
culture.petrodollar.sections.7.title: The flip side: from desert dollars to Mexico's bankruptcy
culture.petrodollar.sections.7.quote: Oil dollars did not stay in the Gulf. They travelled around the world, and came back as debts.
culture.petrodollar.sections.7.paragraph: The Gulf countries could not spend all their revenue at once. A large part was deposited in major Western banks, often as eurodollars in London. These banks, overflowing with liquidity, lent them on in turn, particularly to Latin American countries: their borrowing from American banks rose sharply in the 1970s [8]. This circuit is called ==petrodollar recycling==.

The loans were often at variable rates. When Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve sharply raised its rates to break American inflation, from 1979 onwards, the interest to be paid soared [8]. In August 1982, Mexico's finance minister warned the Fed, the US Treasury and the IMF: Mexico could no longer pay [9].

The danger for Wall Street was immense: at that point, the Latin American debt held by the nine largest American banks amounted to 176% of their capital [9]. Washington and the IMF organised bailouts, in exchange for severe austerity plans. For Latin America, the 1980s became the "lost decade" [8].

The lesson is important: the petrodollar is not just a mechanism that strengthens Washington. ==It links the price of a barrel, the Fed's rates and the debt of countries in the South.== A decision taken in Washington for American inflation can ruin, thousands of kilometres away, countries indebted in dollars.
culture.petrodollar.sections.8.title: Today: the end, or a slow mutation?
culture.petrodollar.sections.8.quote: The death of the petrodollar has been announced a hundred times. It is still here, but it is no longer alone.
culture.petrodollar.sections.8.paragraph: In June 2024, a rumour spread across social media: a 50-year "petrodollar agreement" had supposedly expired on 9 June, and Riyadh had refused to renew it. It is false: no agreement of this kind existed in that form, and in practice Saudi Arabia sold its oil in dollars for decades [13][14].
The financial link, however, still holds: at the end of 2025, Saudi Arabia still held 149.5 billion dollars of American debt, against 137.5 billion a year earlier [15].

But the world has changed. The big oil buyers are now in Asia, Russia sells part of its sanctioned oil in other currencies, and several countries are trying to depend less on the dollar, precisely because Washington uses it as a sanctions weapon (see above, and our course on sanctions). The petrodollar is not dead; it is being challenged, at the margin, by a more multipolar world.

For you, the consequence is very concrete: the price of filling your tank depends on the price of a barrel… expressed in dollars. When the dollar rises against the euro or the Canadian dollar, your fuel costs more, even if the barrel has not moved. That is also the petrodollar: a decision taken in Washington, a tanker in the Gulf, and your bill at the pump.
culture.petrodollar.didYouKnow: When the US Treasury began publishing, month by month, the debt held by each country, it made an exception for Saudi Arabia: its holdings long remained absent from the country-by-country breakdown [6].

culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.sectio: The electric car, a new geopolitical weapon
The battle for the car is no longer fought only at the dealership, but between states.

A century after Ford, the car is once again a matter of power. Batteries need nickel, lithium, cobalt and graphite, and ==the countries that control them use them==. In January 2020, Indonesia, the leading producer of nickel ore, banned its raw export: it wants battery and electric-car factories to set up on its soil [4].

China, which dominates the refining of many metals, hit back on graphite, essential for batteries: announced on 20 October 2023, export controls came into force on 1 December 2023 [5]. Beijing insists they do not target any particular country [5].

The United States closed its market. On 14 May 2024, the White House announced that tariffs on Chinese electric cars would rise from 25% to 100% [6]. A partly symbolic move, economists note, since these cars were already almost absent from the American market [7].

Europe, for its part, hesitates between openness and protection. After an investigation into Chinese subsidies, from 30 October 2024 it imposed, for five years, countervailing duties on electric cars made in China, up to 35.3% for SAIC and the companies that did not cooperate, on top of the usual 10% duty on cars [8].

==The electric car has become an object of rivalry between powers==: metals, factories, subsidies and tariffs. For France, the question "who will build them?" raised above depends as much on these trials of strength as on aid to households.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.6: Storing at other people's: the emergency-oil agreements
A producing country that stores its oil at its customer's is insurance for both.

Reserves are not just a national affair. They give rise to ==agreements between producing and consuming countries==, often discreet ones. Japan is the example: part of its security rests on "joint stocks" with producing countries, the equivalent of 7 days of consumption at the end of 2025 [13].

India has followed the same path. In January 2017, ADNOC signed an agreement with India's strategic reserves agency to store 5.86 million barrels of its crude in the underground caverns of Mangalore, on India's west coast [16].

The agreement grows over time. In May 2026, in the middle of the Hormuz crisis, ADNOC announced it wanted to raise its stocks in India to as much as 30 million barrels [19], and the Emirates are considering storing oil for India at Fujairah, on their coast, outside the strait [19]. In July 2026, the Indian company ONGC announced a new reserve of about 13 million barrels in Mangalore; India then covered only about 9.5 days of its net imports with its strategic reserves [17][18].

The principle is win-win: the producer places its oil near a big customer and benefits from tanks paid for by others; the consumer keeps barrels within reach in case of crisis. ==Reserves become a diplomatic tool== as much as a safety net, just like the collective actions decided within the IEA.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.7: The debates: cost, political use, transition
Insurance you pay for every year, and hesitate to use.

First debate: cost. Storing millions of tonnes ties up money, tanks and caverns, for oil that is almost never used. In France, the bill is paid at the pump [7]; in the United States, the reserve belongs to the federal government [9]. Its defenders reply that it is the price of insurance.

Second debate: what should these stocks be used for? For some, only for real supply disruptions. For others, they can also cushion a price spike. France's use in October 2026, presented as a purchasing-power measure, revived this question [7]. The CEO of SAGESS pointed out in April that these were "not sales" but loans to be returned; the government specifies that a sale remains legally possible [6].

Third debate: replenishment. An emptied stock has to be bought back, ideally when prices are low. In the United States, the administration now proposes to ==lend oil to companies==, 40 million barrels in its latest offer, rather than sell it [11]. Japan, for its part, has to rebuild reserves it drew down heavily in 2026 [13].

Fourth debate: the energy transition. If countries consume less oil, their imports fall, and the 90-day rule mechanically requires smaller stocks. But as long as trucks, planes and tractors run on diesel and kerosene, dependence remains strong, especially for refined products.

Finally, oil is no longer the only energy stored as a precaution. Gas is also stored before winter, under other rules. For you, the lesson is concrete: when a crisis breaks out far from here, part of what happens at the petrol station depends on tanks and caverns you will never see.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.6.ti: Agreements, alliances and small cables: undersea diplomacy
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.6.qu: A cable a few thousand kilometres long can become an affair of state.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.6.pa: The rivalry is not only about the big intercontinental cables. It also lurks in ==small projects== that are almost invisible. In the Pacific, the East Micronesia Cable project, around 73 million dollars, was to link Nauru, Kiribati and the Federated States of Micronesia. The bid from China's HMN (Huawei's former cable branch) was 20% cheaper than those of Alcatel Submarine Networks and Japan's NEC [16].

Washington was worried: the future cable was to connect near another one, HANTRU-1, which serves an American missile-defence test base on Kwajalein atoll. After American warnings, the World Bank-led tender ended in 2021 without an award [16]. In January 2023, the three countries committed to relaunching the project, this time with funding from the United States, Japan and Australia [17].

The great powers also sign ==political agreements==. In September 2024, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, a joint statement proposed by the United States set out nine principles for cable security (trusted suppliers, rapid repairs, route diversity) [18]. Among the first signatories: the European Union, France, Japan, Australia, Canada, but also the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands [18]. Others followed: Italy in October, Norway on 19 November 2024, the day after damage to two Baltic cables [19].

China has its own routes. The PEACE cable, owned by a subsidiary of the Chinese group Hengtong, links Pakistan to France via Egypt, Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya and the Seychelles; it landed in Marseille in October 2021, with Orange as its partner in France [20]. Its first segments went into service on 22 December 2022 [21]. It is one of the building blocks of the "digital silk roads".

Europe responds with its own projects. The Medusa cable, presented as the first digital project of the EU's "Global Gateway" programme, is to link both shores of the Mediterranean over about 8,700 km, with 19 landing points and a connection for every North African country; the EU put in a 40-million-euro grant, channelled through the European Investment Bank [22]. In December 2025, it reached Nador, in Morocco [23]. ==Every cable laid is also a choice of alliance.==
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.6.bo: The United States and allies: pressure against Chinese suppliers, funding for cables in the Pacific, the New York statement (2024) [16][17][18].
China: cables such as PEACE, from Asia to Marseille via East Africa [20].
European Union: Medusa, between Europe and North Africa, and the 2025 action plan for cable security [1][22].
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.7.qu: The law of the sea requires punishment, but gives few means to act far from the coast.
culture.cables-sous-marins.sections.7.pa: Offshore, cables are protected by an old body of law. The 1884 Paris Convention for the Protection of Submarine Telegraph Cables inspired Article 113 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea [15].

This article requires states to make the breaking or damaging of a cable an offence. But it does not give them the power to take action against foreign ships on the high seas [15]. In other words: a country can have its cable cut far from its shores without being able to stop the suspect ship.

States therefore react in other ways. In January 2025, NATO launched the =="Baltic Sentry"== mission: warships, maritime patrol aircraft and naval drones to monitor the Baltic and deter sabotage [12].

On 21 February 2025, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs presented an ==action plan on cable security==. It covers telecommunication cables and power cables, around four strands: prevention, detection, response and repair, deterrence. Deterrence includes sanctions against hostile actors and the "shadow fleet" [1].

The other response is economic: multiplying routes so that one cut cable does not cut everything, and building new repair ships. A damaged cable remains useless as long as no ship can go and repair it [9].

For you, these cables are invisible, but they are behind every streamed video, every payment to a foreign website, every video call with the other side of the world. In well-served regions, a cut usually means a slowdown while traffic is rerouted, as in the Red Sea in 2024 [10]. But for an island linked by a single cable, like Tonga in 2022, a cut can stop everything [11].
To watch: the renewal of the repair fleet, the investigations in the Baltic and Taiwan, and the race between the United States and China to lay tomorrow's cables.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.t: When the Nile redraws the alliances of the Horn of Africa
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.q: The dam is no longer negotiated only around a table: it weighs on every alliance in the region.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.p: In the absence of an agreement on water, everyone is looking for allies. On 2 March 2021, Egypt and Sudan signed a military cooperation agreement: training, border security, counter-terrorism, military industries [16][17]. Four days later, in Khartoum, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi rejected any attempt to "control the Blue Nile through unilateral measures" [16].

On 1 January 2024, Ethiopia, landlocked since Eritrea's independence, signed with Somaliland, a breakaway territory that no one recognises, a memorandum meant to give it access to the Red Sea. Somalia rejected it the very next day as an attack on its sovereignty [18]. Cairo immediately took Mogadishu's side [19].

On 10 October 2024, the presidents of Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia met in Asmara. They committed to better protecting Somalia's land and sea borders [20]. For many analysts, it is an ==axis meant to put pressure on Ethiopia==, including over the dam [21]. Turkey then acted as mediator: in the Ankara Declaration of 11 December 2024, Ethiopia and Somalia agreed on commercial access to the sea that respects Somali sovereignty [22].

A paradox: on the same 1 January 2024, Egypt and Ethiopia joined the BRICS together, the club of large emerging countries around China, India, Brazil, Russia and South Africa [23]. Two Nile rivals now sit at the same table.

And the game goes on: in October 2026, Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia met again and rejected any "unilateral measure" that would harm the water rights of Egypt and Sudan [24]. ==The dam is no longer just a question of water: it is a thread that links all the tensions of the Horn of Africa.==
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.6.b: On Egypt's side: Sudan (2021 military agreement), then Eritrea and Somalia (Asmara summit, 2024) [16][20].
On Ethiopia's side: the agreement with Somaliland for access to the sea, disputed by Somalia [18].
The mediators: the United States in 2020, the African Union, then Turkey between Ethiopia and Somalia in 2024 [22].
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.7.t: What the Nile says about water wars
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.7.q: More than a water war, the Nile is the example of a water peace that cannot manage to be written.
culture.barrage-renaissance.sections.7.p: Despite the strong words, the Nile has not seen open war over the dam. The conflict is played out with treaties, statements at the UN, mediation and flow figures. This is often the case: water strains relations more than it starts wars.

The case shows first that ==geography gives power==. The country that controls the source can build without asking permission. But the downstream country has other assets: its diplomatic weight, its alliances, its army, and the long history of its uses.

It also shows that ==international water law remains vague==. Two principles clash: "equitable and reasonable" use, invoked upstream, and the ban on causing "significant harm", put forward downstream. Both appear in the 2015 declaration [4], but no judge is responsible for reconciling them.

Finally, the climate changes the game. No one knows when the next long drought will hit the Ethiopian highlands. The day it comes, the question will no longer be "should there be a dam?" but =='who keeps the water when there is not enough for everyone?'== [8].
The Renaissance Dam is now built. The debate is no longer about its existence, but about its operating rules. The Nile remains a shared river; it is its management that is not yet shared.
